design_principles.principle: News should hit a price you can watch
design_principles.app_approach: A live event-study lab: fire an announcement and compare efficient (jump), underreaction (drift), overreaction (reversal) — then overlay the real Keown–Pinkerton takeover path.
Simulate random walks and feel the drift/volatility cone; then hunt for autocorrelation in your own simulated data and discover how weak the evidence in T months really is.
The size decile table, the January bar chart, and the DeBondt–Thaler curves ship with the actual figures from the deck — students explore evidence, not cartoons.

design_principles.principle: End on the best story in finance
design_principles.app_approach: A 3Com/Palm stub calculator: type the two prices, watch the market value a profitable business at −$25 billion, then walk the stub back to zero along the real 2000 timeline.

slides.title: Prices Are Forecasts
slides.content_summary: P = E[Σ discounted dividends]. Interactive DCF: dividend and discount-rate dials move the price; a 'news' button shocks cash flows and the price jumps instantly. The hidden assumption: 'correct' presumes a pricing model.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Raise the discount rate with dividends fixed — why did the price fall if nothing about cash flows changed?'

slides.title: Three Forms, One Paradox, One Trap
slides.content_summary: Nested information sets ⟹ weak/semi-strong/strong. Grossman–Stiglitz: efficiency only up to information + trading costs. The joint hypothesis problem: efficiency is never tested alone.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'If rejecting a test can always be blamed on the model, what evidence COULD move you?'

slides.title: How Fast Is the Market? The Event Study
slides.content_summary: CAR around announcements, averaged over firms. Toggle efficient / underreaction / overreaction paths; overlay the real Keown–Pinkerton takeover data: run-up (leakage), jump from ~12% to ~26% at t=0, flat after.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'The price ran up for 20 days BEFORE the announcement. Which form of efficiency does that threaten — weak, semi-strong, or strong?'

problem_spec.scenario: Market model with α=0, β=1.2. Around the announcement: day −1: stock +0.5%, market +0.4%; day 0: stock +6.0%, market +1.0%; day +1: stock +0.2%, market 0.0%.

slides.title: Martingales and Random Walks
slides.content_summary: Martingale: E[P_{t+1}|history]=P_t — the fair game, but risk-blind. RW1: P_t=μ+P_{t−1}+ε; mean μt, variance σ²t. RW2/RW3 weaken iid to independence to mere uncorrelatedness (volatility clustering lives in RW3). Simulate paths, drag drift and σ, watch the cone.

slides.title: Hunting for Autocorrelation
slides.content_summary: Set a true ρ, simulate T months, and see how often you'd detect it (SE≈1/√T). The puzzle: individual stocks slightly negative, portfolios positive — the decomposition shows cross-autocovariances (large stocks lead small) must be large and positive. Microstructure caveats.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Your portfolio autocorrelation is positive while every stock's own autocorrelation is negative. Where is the predictability hiding?'

slides.title: Your Turn: How Big Is Small Predictability?

problem_spec.scenario: Monthly returns, iid variance. Estimated first-order autocorrelation γ1 = 0.10 with T = 400 months (SE ≈ 1/√T).
problem_spec.verification: Variance explained = ρ² = 0.01 ⟹ 1.0%. SE = 1/√400 = 0.05 ⟹ t = 0.10/0.05 = 2.0 — statistically borderline, economically tiny.

slides.title: The Anomaly Recipe — and Its Three Readings
slides.content_summary: Anomaly = characteristic-sorted strategy that beats the market's Sharpe. Recipe: sort, measure, subtract costs. Then triage: risk (payoffs in bad times — consumption logic), inefficiency, or data mining (peso problems lurk).

slides.title: Where Do Factors Come From?
slides.content_summary: APT (factor structure + no arbitrage, silent on identity) vs ICAPM (state variables, named). Three hunting methods: statistical (PCA: top eigenvectors of Ω̂; ~5 factors suffice), macro (CRR 1986 five), characteristics (FF SMB/HML). Each with advantage/disadvantage.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'CRR motivate macro factors with the APT. What's uncomfortable about that?' (APT prices covariance-matrix factors; macro series needn't drive it.)

slides.title: Your Turn: Read the CRR Table

problem_spec.scenario: Chen–Roll–Ross report the industrial-production (MP) premium as 11.756, in units of percent per month × 10 (1958–84, t = 3.05).
problem_spec.verification: Annual premium = 11.756 × 12 / 10 = 14.11 ⟹ ≈14.1% per year (vs ≈6.5% for the market premium).

slides.title: The Anomaly Gallery (Original Numbers)
slides.content_summary: Four tabs with the deck's real data: SIZE (deciles 19.8%→11.9%, betas 1.17→0.95); JANUARY (0.70% Jan bar vs the rest; 3/4 in the first five days); CONTRARIAN (DeBondt–Thaler loser +0.30 / winner −0.10 CARs over 60 months); MOMENTUM & VALUE (the strategies and their dueling readings).
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Contrarian says losers win over 3–5 years; momentum says winners win over 3–12 months. Reconcile them.'

slides.title: Why Doesn't Arbitrage Fix It?
slides.content_summary: Shleifer's three defenses of efficiency and their three rebuttals. The limits: no close substitutes, drawdowns, short horizons, costs, short-sale constraints. Shleifer–Vishny: clients pull money after losses — arbitrage capital vanishes exactly when mispricing widens. Plus the data-mining histogram (≈5 of 100 random series look 'significant').

slides.title: The −$25 Billion Business: 3Com/Palm
slides.content_summary: Stub calculator: 3Com $81.81, Palm $95.06, ratio 1.5 ⟹ stub −$60.78/share. Trade: buy 1 3Com, short 1.5 Palm, wait for the announced spin-off. The real stub timeline 3/2–9/18/00 with the 3/20, 5/8 (IRS) and 7/27 (distribution) events. Table of the six negative stubs.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Why did the announced intention to spin off matter so much for the trade?'

problem_spec.scenario: Parent trades at $50 and owns 0.8 shares of the carved-out issuer per parent share; the issuer trades at $80. Separately, Lamont–Thaler back out a 14% cost of shorting Palm over two months.

slides.title: Prices Can Be Wrong Without Being Exploitable
slides.content_summary: Parents beat issuers by 33% over ~6 months; put–call parity massively violated; borrowing Palm cost ≈119%/yr. Fama's operational definition tolerates it all — a stock can be infinitely overpriced with infinite shorting costs and the market stays 'efficient'. Closing triage for any predictability: rational premia, limited-arbitrage mispricing, or chance.

new_problem_templates.answer_rule: stub = P_parent − ratio × P_issuer; annualized cost = (1+c)^(12/m) − 1
